content: This is the second update of a Cochrane review originally published in 2009. Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN) is a rare but treatable condition that originates in the fetal chorion during pregnancy. Most women with low-risk GTN can be cured through uterine evacuation, with or without the use of single-agent chemotherapy. However, chemotherapy protocols differ across treatment centers worldwide, and the relative benefits and risks of these regimens remain unclear. The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of first-line chemotherapy in the treatment of low-risk GTN. To achieve this, electronic searches were conducted in the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, and Embase databases in September 2008, February 2012, and January 2016. Online trial registries were also searched for protocols and ongoing trials. For the original review, randomized controlled trials (RCTs), quasi-RCTs, and non-RCTs were included. However, in this updated review, only RCTs were considered. Two independent reviewers assessed the studies for inclusion and extracted data using a pre-designed data extraction form. Meta-analysis was performed using a random-effects model. Seven RCTs involving 667 women were included in this updated review. Most of the studies had a low or moderate risk of bias. All trials compared methotrexate with actinomycin D. Specifically, three studies compared weekly intramuscular (IM) methotrexate with bi-weekly pulsed intravenous (IV) actinomycin D (393 women). One study compared a five-day IM methotrexate regimen with bi-weekly pulsed IV actinomycin D (75 women). Another study compared an eight-day IM methotrexate-folinic acid (MTX-FA) regimen with a five-day IV actinomycin D regimen (49 women). One additional study compared an eight-day IM MTX-FA regimen with bi-weekly pulsed IV actinomycin D. One study did not contribute any data. Moderate-certainty evidence suggests that actinomycin D is likely more effective in achieving a primary cure compared to methotrexate (risk ratio [RR] 0.65, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.57 to 0.75; six trials, 577 participants; I² = 26%). Methotrexate treatment is more likely to fail compared to actinomycin D (RR 3.55, 95% CI 1.81 to 6.95; six trials, 577 participants; I² = 61%; moderate-certainty evidence). Low-certainty evidence indicates that there may be little or no difference between methotrexate and actinomycin D in terms of nausea (four studies, 466 women; RR 0.61, 95% CI 0.29 to 1.26) or other individual side effects. However, the data for these outcomes were insufficient and inconsistent, making definitive conclusions difficult. Low-certainty evidence also suggests that there may be little or no difference in the risk of severe adverse events (SAEs) between the two treatment groups overall (five studies, 515 women; RR 0.35, 95% CI 0.08 to 1.66; I² = 60%). However, the direction of the effect appears to favor methotrexate, and additional evidence is required. Subgroup analyses suggest that actinomycin D may be associated with a higher risk of SAEs compared to methotrexate, although this is based on low-certainty evidence. No evidence was found regarding the impact of these treatments on future fertility. In conclusion, actinomycin D is likely more effective in achieving a primary cure and less likely to result in treatment failure compared to methotrexate in women with low-risk GTN. There may be little or no difference in side effects between the two regimens, but actinomycin D may carry a higher risk of severe adverse events. Higher-certainty evidence is still needed to guide the treatment of low-risk GTN. Four ongoing trials are expected to provide valuable insights in this area. Given the diversity of treatment regimens, the findings from these trials could enable a network meta-analysis in future reviews, helping women and clinicians make more informed decisions about the optimal treatment for low-risk GTN.
